title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
hints: postorder always visits the root last - so the very last element of postorder tells you the value of the current subtree's root immediately

once you know the root's value, find that same value's position in the inorder slice you're working with - everything to its left in inorder is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree
precompute a value -> index map over inorder once, so you don't rescan it for every recursive call

process the right subtree before the left subtree when consuming postorder from the end, since postorder lists left, then right, then root - so working backwards from the end you see root, then right, then left
build the result directly into a growable flat array at the correct heap index, rather than building a linked node tree and converting afterward
commonMistakes: consuming postorder from the front instead of the back, since the root is at the end, not the start
recursing into the left subtree before the right subtree when peeling elements off the end of postorder, which desyncs which element is 'consumed' next
rescanning inorder with a linear search for every node instead of precomputing a value -> index map, which is correct but needlessly slow
off-by-one errors in the inorder slice boundaries when splitting into left and right sub-ranges

content.problemStatement:
Binary trees in these problems are encoded as a flat array named `tree`
using complete-binary-tree (heap) indexing:

- the root sits at index 0
- a node at index `i` has its left child at index `2*i+1` and right child at index `2*i+2`
- any position at or beyond the end of the array, or holding the sentinel value `-101`, means "no node there"
- real node values are always in the range -100 to 100, so -101 can never be mistaken for a genuine value

You're given two arrays describing a single binary tree, both listing
only the real (non-missing) nodes and with no sentinels: `inorder`, the
sequence of values visited by an inorder traversal (left subtree, then
the node, then right subtree), and `postorder`, the sequence visited by a
postorder traversal (left subtree, then right subtree, then the node).

**Rebuild the tree that produced these traversals, and return it using the flat array encoding described above.**

All values across both arrays are distinct, and there's exactly one tree consistent with both traversals.
constraints: both arrays describe the same tree and contain the same distinct values
there is exactly one binary tree consistent with the given traversals
notes: a tree that is a straight left-leaning or right-leaning chain (every node has only one child)

sampleTestCases.explanation: postorder's last element, 3, is the root; everything before 3's position in inorder ([9]) forms the left subtree, everything after ([15, 20, 7]) forms the right subtree, and the same logic recurses into each side
a single node has no traversal ambiguity at all
postorder's last element 1 is the root; in inorder, 1 comes before 2, so the entire remaining value 2 forms the right subtree and there is no left subtree

optimal.time: O(n), building an index map once and doing O(1) lookups per node
optimal.space: O(n) for the index map, recursion stack, and output tree
optimal.pattern: divide and conquer using the last element of postorder as the root

bruteForce.approach: same recursive divide-and-conquer as the optimal approach, but find the root's position in inorder with a linear scan every time instead of a precomputed lookup
bruteForce.time: O(n^2) worst case (a linear scan per recursive call, over n calls)
bruteForce.space: O(n) for the recursion and the rebuilt tree
